title: 2026 San Juan National Forest Prescribed Fire Program
field_incident_overview:
Spring Prescribed Fire Operations Are Complete.

The prescribed fire program will continue in Fall of 2026 as conditions allow.

The forests in Southwest Colorado are part of a fire-adapted ecosystem, which historically experienced frequent, low intensity fires on a large scale. Prescribed fire replicates that fire regime and increases the area on our landscape that has been burned at low and moderate conditions. These efforts reduce hazardous ground fuels, lessen the risk of unplanned large-scale wildfire, help restore ponderosa pine ecosystems, and improve wildlife habitat. Prescribed fire also reduces the ladder fuels that can carry fire into the canopy, killing mature trees. Prescribed fire smoke may affect your health. For more information, visit Wood smoke and your health.

Columbine Ranger District: 

The Columbine Ranger District will continue the following prescribed fire projects in Fall of 2026 as conditions allow. Smoke will be visible from Arboles, Bayfield, Pagosa Springs, as well as the U.S. Highway 160 and 151 corridors near those towns.

  • Sauls Creek: This project area includes multiple potential units totaling approximately 900 acres. This project is located in Sauls Creek near NFSR 608, east of Bayfield and south of Highway 160 in La Plata County. It is part of a larger fuels reduction strategy that has included commercial logging and other fuels reduction work. The Columbine Ranger District completed 255 acres on the Sauls Creek prescribed fire project March 28-29, 2026 and another 314 acres on April 24-25, 2026. 
  • Southern HDs Prescribed Fire: This project is approximately 2,000 acres in the Fosset Gulch area (NFSR 613), west of Chimney Rock National Monument in Archuleta County. Units will be burned using ground ignitions and possibly unmanned aircraft systems (drones) as well. In past years the Columbine District burned adjacent units to help reduce wildfire risk to local homes and infrastructure.

Pagosa Ranger District:

The Pagosa Ranger District will continue the following prescribed fire projects in Fall of 2026 as conditions allow.

  • Brockover-Devil Prescribed Fire: This 2,100-acre project area consists of "maintenance" burning, further reducing ground and ladder fuels. This treatment will build on the 2025 fall prescribed fire operations in the area and complement numerous mastication, thinning, and timber harvest treatments. These units are located along NFSR 629 and 923, west of Pagosa Springs and north of Highway 160. The Pagosa Ranger District completed 1,365 acres of this prescribed fire project April 23, 2026.
  • Echo Canyon Prescribed Fire: This 1,139-acre project is located along NFSR 029 southeast of Pagosa Springs and east of Highway 84. In 2018, this project area was the site of commercial thinning, followed by mastication work in 2021 and prescribed fire in 2023. This year, the District hopes to conduct a "maintenance" burn to maximize fuel reduction benefits. 
  • Eight Mile Mesa Prescribed Fire: This project is located on Eight Mile Mesa (NFSR 651), south of Pagosa Springs and west of Highway 84. 275 acres will be burned to clean up slash and forest litter following a 2022 oak mastication project as well as other hazardous fuels and timber harvest activities.

Dolores Ranger District: 

The Dolores Ranger District will continue the following prescribed fire projects in Fall of 2026 as conditions allow. During burning operations, smoke may be visible around Mancos, Dolores, Dove Creek, Cortez, and Highway 491 between Dove Creek and Pleasant View. Smoke may settle into low lying valleys and the Dolores River Canyon overnight.

  • Salter-Carlyle Prescribed Fire: This project is located 15 miles east of Cahone, near Salter Y along NFSR 510 in Montezuma and Dolores Counties. The Dolores Ranger District completed 1,660 acres on the Salter-Carlyle Prescribed Fire on May 20.
  • Boggy Draw Prescribed Fire: This 4,107-acre project is located 4-8 miles northeast of Dolores in Montezuma County, along NFSR 526 and 527. Smaller units of this overall project will be implemented as weather and conditions allow (see map). The Dolores Ranger District completed 1,586 acres on the Boggy Draw Prescribed Fire on April 219-20. The area closure was lifted on April 24.

title: Coconino National Forest Prescribed Burn Projects
field_incident_description:
Prescribed burns are important part of forest restoration and protecting communities by creating buffers around them. Prescribed burns and mechanical thinning work together to remove fuels such as woody debris and logging scraps from the forest floor during times of opportune weather.

Fire managers make every effort to effectively plan and execute burn plans at times when weather allows for smoke impacts to be minimized and transport up and over communities. If you have a complaint about the smoke impacts you are experiencing from any of the prescribed burn projects and would like to talk to a member of Fire Management Leadership, please call our hotline at 928-226-4608 and leave your message with your name and number and someone will return your call as soon as they are able.

title: Billy Fire
field_incident_overview:
This is the final update of the Type 3 team as they transfer command of the fire back to the local district as of tomorrow morning. 64 personnel remain assigned to the Billy Fire.

Unless there are significant changes in fire activity, this will be the last daily update of the Billy Fire.

-

The Billy Fire is a lightning-caused wildfire on the Tonto National Forest, 15 miles south of Young, Arizona. Firefighters are taking a full suppression strategy on the fire situated on the east side of the Sierra Ancha Mountains.

title: Elk RBX Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Elk fire was discovered on Saturday, August 2nd as a lightning strike on private land in the Oak Ridge area. Drought with severe and extreme weather conditions along with two days of red flag warning caused heightened fire activity. Residences were evacuated from the area. As weather conditions changed and remained favorable for the Elk Fire, crews were able to gain substantial line around the Elk Fire. 

The Elk Fire is currently reported as being 100% contained.

title: 2026  Huron-Manistee NFs Spring/Summer Prescribed Fire Season
field_incident_overview:
The Huron-Manistee National Forests Fire and Aviation Management Unit is preparing for prescribed fire operations.

Rx burns are planned events that are matched to predetermined weather/fuel parameters. We will evaluate weather conditions in the hours before a burn begins. If conditions warrant, scheduled prescribed fire activities may be canceled. Updates including cancellations, additions and corrections will be added to this post.

Prescribed fires reduce risk to the public by removing hazardous vegetation to mitigate wildfires and prevent loss of property. They also help to re-establish fire’s positive role in local ecosystems, increase native plant regeneration and improve wildlife habitat and forest health. 

During active burning, smoke and flames may be visible from roads and in areas downwind of the burn site. Residents may experience smoke during the prescribed burns. When driving, slow down and turn on your headlights when you encounter smoke on the road. For more detailed information about air quality, go to AirNow online or download the app. 

Residents and motorists may also encounter roadblocks, specially trained fire personnel and heavy equipment, such as engines and dozers, performing Rx Fire operations. 

The planned prescribed fires listed below are organized by ranger district, county and township. Respective recreational trails and sites may close for public safety. Watch for warning signs along roads near all prescribed fire areas before and during burns. 

Stay informed about the scheduled prescribed fires through the forest website, social media channels, and InciWeb, the interagency incident information system. We will notify county emergency management officials when burning begins. If you wish to be notified about prescribed fires in your vicinity, contact your nearest District Ranger Office.

Firefighters will monitor the burn area for days following the burn.

title: Poorman Prescribed (Rx) Fire
field_incident_overview:
Update: Poorman Prescribed Fire (June 30 at 4:00 p.m.)

The area received 1.7 inches of rain over the past weekend along with below average temperatures. The warming and drying trend is expected to return Thursday with temperatures predicted to rise into the upper 80s and low 90s by the end of the week.

After the wetting rain event, fire activity and smoke impacts remain minimal. Highway 17/Banks-Lowman Road remained free of debris over the weekend, but crews will continue to patrol for potential rollout. The Bear River Wildland Fire Module will be on the unit throughout the week and will also be available for Initial Attack response should the need arise.

For questions about the Poorman Prescribed Fire, call 208-861-3465

Background
The Poorman Prescribed Fire is a 2,692‑acre fuels‑reduction project designed to lower the risk of high‑intensity wildfire near the communities of Crouch and Garden Valley. This area has been successfully treated with prescribed fire in the past, including the late 1990s and again from 2010–2012.

This project is one of several active forest management efforts on the Boise National Forest to reduce wildfire risk and support firefighter safety. In spring 2026, seven prescribed burns were successfully implemented across the Boise National Forest.

Ignitions for the Poorman Prescribed Fire took place over four days from late April through early May. Firefighters have worked daily to patrol the control line to reinforce it against any nearby fire activity that could possibly threaten it. The fire has been meeting treatment objectives, consuming pine needles, downed logs, brush, and some grasses. However, unusually dry weather in May has led to smoke lingering in the Garden Valley area longer than anticipated.

Current Situation
Due to ongoing dry conditions and continued smoke impacts, firefighters are taking additional steps to reduce fuels and shorten the duration of smoke in the area:

• Perimeter work: Beginning June 2, firefighters widened the existing handline around the project boundary by carefully burning grasses along the edge. This work was completed on June 3 and further reduces the likelihood of fire moving outside the project area.

• Interior burning: Firefighters will be burning remaining grasses inside the project area starting June 4, with work expected to continue for up to four days. This may temporarily increase smoke but will help reduce future smoke production and speed up the overall clean‑up period.

Going Forward

This InciWeb site will be updated regularly while the prescribed fire is being patrolled. For questions about the Poorman Prescribed Fire, call 208-861-3465

title: Santa Rosa Island Burned Area Emergency Response (BAER)
field_incident_description:
On Friday, May 15, 2026, an aircraft flying over Santa Rosa Island in Channel Islands National Park reported a wildfire. National Park Service (NPS) staff already on the island confirmed it later that morning. The Santa Rosa Island Fire was located on the southeastern end of the island in remote and rugged terrain. This was a full-suppression human-caused wildfire and remains under investigation. The fire was fully contained on June 4.

A team of Burned Area Emergency Response (BAER) specialists were on the island through June 5-10, evaluating post-fire conditions and identifying immediate risks. The team includes engineers, ecologists, hydrologists, archaeologists, and wildland fire specialists who will assess soil stability, watershed conditions, infrastructure damage, threats to natural and cultural resources, and other post-fire impacts. Their findings will help guide emergency stabilization efforts and inform decisions about public access.
field_incident_overview:
Current Conditions:
On 6/16, the Burned Area Emergency Response (BAER) team presented their recommendations and funding specifications to Channel Islands National Park staff. These emergency stabilization recommendations will will help park staff prioritize actions needed to reduce risks including erosion, flooding, hazardous trees, and impacts to sensitive resources. Using information collected during their evaluations, the team identified immediate threats to life, safety, property, and critical natural and cultural resources that may be caused by the fire. While the park will implement time-sensitive projects over the summer, many projects will last for years, as the island recovers from the fire.
 

Closures:
Santa Rosa Island is closed to all day and overnight use through at least June 30, 2026, due to the wildfire. All Water Canyon Campground reservations have been cancelled through this date and visitors have been notified by email. Campground reservation holders with bookings through August 14, 2026, have also been informed that the wildfire may affect their stay. If additional cancellations are needed, they will receive follow-up emails.

Backcountry camping within the southeastern quadrant of Santa Rosa Island will remain closed for the remainder of the 2026 recreation season.

title: South Fork Fire
field_incident_overview:
The South Fork Fire ignited on June 9, 2026, in the Soldier Creek Wilderness area of the Nebraska National Forest’s Pine Ridge Ranger District near Crawford, Nebraska. Local responders, U.S. Forest Service crews and volunteer firefighting partners engaged the fire early as dry fuels, steep terrain and strong winds drove rapid spread. U.S. Highway 20 was closed by the Nebraska Department of Transportation as the fire jumped the highway. A red flag warning was in effect through Wednesday, June 10.

By June 10, the fire had grown to nearly 9,000 acres and Nebraska’s Governor Pillen officially issued an emergency declaration for the South Fork Fire. It was fueled by rugged terrain, dry vegetation including timber and grassy undergrowth, and strong winds. On June 11 at 6 am the Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2, under the command of Jay Mickey, assumed control of the fire.

On June 12, containment increased to 7% even as the fire grew to about 28,067 acres. Resources including National Guard units, ground crews, dozers and aircraft focused on defending the towns of Crawford and the Fort Robinson State Park area. The Red Cross established community shelter options at the Chadron State College–Andrews Hall.

By June 15, containment was at 55% and the fire had grown to 38,914 acres. 581 personnel were supporting the fire. Forecasters predicted that the week ahead would bring sustained winds anticipated between 23 and 30 miles per hour, and the possibility of gusts escalating to as high as 50 miles per hour. 

Nebraska’s Governor, Jim Pillen received an operational visit of the South Fork Fire on June 16. He visited ICP and was provided with a comprehensive briefing. He had the opportunity to communicate with members of his constituency as well as incident team members. 

Containment reached 80% on June 17, with the acres climbing to 39,057. Although conditions continued to change, fire activity was generally quiet. A NIROPS flight (a thermal imaging aircraft used to map active wildfires) was ordered after several areas of hot spots were discovered. 

Line is now in place around the entire fire perimeter. Crews are working to secure and mop up the containment line and will continue for several days. Suppression repair work is also u begin underway and will continue in the next few days. 

On June 20th the overall acreage of the South Fork Fire increased to 39,696 due to more accurate satellite mapping showing previously unseen grassy areas and containment increased to 90%.

Rocky Mountain CIMT2 transfered command to the Nebraska Type 3 team on Sunday, June 21, 2026, at 6 p.m.  

Please follow the Nebraska National Forest on Facebook and the Nebraska National Forest website's Alerts and Notices page for further updates.

field_incident_overview:

Firefighters will continue mop up operations and perimeter patrols to secure containment lines and keep the fire within the established perimeter. Fuels consist primarily of medium logging slash, brush, and tall grasses.

A Red Flag Warning remains in effect through Sunday evening, with dry breezy conditions and near-critical fire weather expected to continue into next week. Gusty winds may produce interior flare ups and localized spotting potential over the next 72 hours; however, no current threat to communities, infrastructure, or other values at risk has been identified.

There has been no reported damage to structures or infrastructure, no civilian impacts. Approximately 192 personnel remain assigned to the incident in support of suppression and containment efforts.

Operational priorities remained focused on patrolling and securing the fire perimeter, completing mop-up where needed, implementing suppression repair, and maintaining containment.

field_incident_description: The fire is burning in the west side of Olympic National Park on a steep, densely forested slope approximately 5 miles west-northwest of Mount Olympus.
field_incident_overview:
Situation: The lightning-caused Mt. Tom Creek Fire is burning high on a remote mountain slope on the west side of Olympic National Park. The area is in steep, densely forested terrain approximately five miles west‑northwest of Mount Olympus. Backpackers first reported the fire on June 24th.

The fire is approximately six miles from the Hoh Rain Forest administrative site. The Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, campground, and trails all remain open to the public.

Firefighters are using indirect confinement tactics as part of a full-suppression strategy. These tactics include removing vegetation around recreation and administrative infrastructure and using helicopters to drop water to cool host spots and keep the fire within its current footprint. The fire is constrained by natural features on a couple flanks, where fire managers have determined it is 27% contained.

High relative humidity and periodic precipitation may constrain fire behavior, but are unlikely to extinguish the fire.

Smoke: Smoke may be visible from various locations on the Olympic Peninsula. Air quality can change quickly.  For current smoke information, visit: https://fire.airnow.gov

Fire Restrictions: Olympic National Park implemented fire restrictions June 25th. Dispersed and backcountry fires are prohibited. Fires within established metal fire rings in developed campgrounds and picnic areas are exempt from this prohibition. Propane and gas stoves are allowed, if operated at least three feet away from flammable vegetation and forest litter.

Air Space Restrictions: A Temporary Flight Restriction is in place. If you fly, we can’t. Every time a drone is spotted near the fire all aircraft are grounded until we can be sure the drone is clear of this area: http://knowbeforeyoufly.org

title: Wild Goose Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Wild Goose Fire began on June 26, 2026 just south of Wild Goose Canyon on the Fishlake National Forest. It is located east of Holden and south of Scipio, Utah. The fire burned in mixed fuel types and steep terrain. The fire grew very quickly in the first 24 hours, prompting evacuations of nearby communities and a closure order on Fishlake National Forest.

In the first days of the incident, cooler temperatures allowed firefighters to actively engage the fire, installing containment and contingency lines before increased temperatures and heavier winds created critical fire weather conditions. 

Fuels are exceptionally dry for this time of year and contributed to extreme fire behavior, but the lines created in the first week of GBT7's tenure have held and largely curtailed fire spread. Since July 3, fire behavior has remained moderate. On July 10, all evacuation orders were lifted and the Fishlake National Forest Closure was reduced in size to reopen popular recreation areas to the south of the fire.

On July 11 at 1900, command of the fire transitioned back to a local Type 4 Incident Commander on the Fishlake National Forest.

title: Gold Mountain Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Gold Mountain Fire was discovered on June 27, 2026, at approximately 5:33 pm 2 miles northeast of Ouray, CO. Fire initially started burning in mixed conifer vegetation located on inaccessible terrain above the east side of Highway 550. Local, State, and Federal initial attack fire resources were ordered immediately. The fire spread quickly running up steep slopes. A local Type 3 Incident Management Team was assigned on June 27, 2026. Aviation resources were ordered throughout the next day, but high winds and terrain features shut down the use of aviation resources. Fire became very active, with group torching and crowning, increasing the fire growth to the east by 2,000 acres. Fire resources provided public safety and worked to protect structures. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 3 was ordered on June 28, 2026, and took command on June 29, 2026, at 6 pm.  Red Flag conditions over the following week led to extreme fire behavior increasing the fire growth to over 30,000 acres by July 6, 2026. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2 assumed command July 14, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 1 assumed command July 26, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2 assumed command again on August 9th, 2026 of both the Gold Mountain and Elk Fires following a coordinated planned transition. On August 22nd, 2026 Crawford Incident Management Team Type 3 assumed command. 

Firefighters are using a risk-based suppression strategy that prioritizes public and firefighter safety while protecting communities, critical infrastructure, water systems and access along the Highway 550 corridor. Where direct engagement is unsafe or impractical, firefighters are using natural features, indirect containment lines, point protection around homes and other values at risk, and pumps, hoses and large water tanks to support structure protection. title: Sacaton Fire
field_incident_overview:
Background: On the afternoon of Sunday, June 21, the Mogollon Baldy lookout detected a lightning-caused fire on Sacaton Mountain (elevation 10,658 feet) in the Gila Wilderness. The fire, which is on the Glenwood Ranger District, was initially about 4.5 miles west of the lookout tower. 

Firefighters quickly conducted an aerial assessment and estimated the fire—burning in brush, timber, logs, and snags—was about 2 acres and exhibiting moderate fire behavior. By late evening, the lookout reported the fire had grown to approximately 4 acres.

The fire’s location presents extreme risks to both ground and aerial firefighters: It is burning among numerous snags, a dense tangle of fallen trees, and thick brush regeneration from the 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire. The landscape is very rugged and steep (e.g., 40–60 percent slopes). Safety zones and escape routes are nonexistent. Emergency extraction times would be unacceptably long (i.e., 6+ hours) and logistically difficult. High-elevation flying, especially during hot weather, is very hazardous and an unacceptable transfer of risk to the pilot.

Smoke & Air Quality: Smoke is visible from numerous areas in and surrounding the Gila National Forest. Scroll down for air quality information and the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map.

title: Biscar
field_incident_description: Wildland Fire
field_incident_overview:
Links - Daily Update (pdf)     |     Daily Informational Map (pdf)     |     Fire Progression Map    |     Daily Operations Update (video) 

 

The Biscar Fire started from a lightning strike on July 18, 2026 within Lassen County.  It grew quickly with warm temperatures and strong winds pushing it eastward across Highway 395.  It is currently mapped at 69,352 acres with 97% containment.

Fire Activity: Fire activity has been minimal despite elevated fire weather conditions. Containment lines around the fire continue to be reinforced. Crews have been checking integrity of the containment lines using a tactic called “cold trailing,” where fire fighters walk along these lines to verify that no heat persists. 

About 200 firefighters were released Sunday, and additional 200 were released Monday and made available to other fires in the region.  Resources continue to be made available for reassignments today as they finish their tasks on the Biscar Fire.  A National Preparedness Level 5 (Highest Level) indicates a significant amount of fire activity nationally with resources (crews, engines, aircraft) mostly being committed; and therefore fewer resources available to respond to new ignitions.

California Interagency Incident Management Team 3 has demobilized from the Biscar Fire today, and will be reassigned to the Castle Fire in southern Oregon.  The Team thanks the residents and Emergency Management staff of Lassen County, CA and Washoe County, NV for their support and dedication during the Biscar Fire.

Why the strange name?  Fires are often named after geographic features near the fire, and in this case, Biscar Reservoir is located just a few miles south of where the fire was first reported.  Pierre “Pete” Biscar (1881–1947),  was a French-born rancher who settled in Secret Valley, California, and constructed the first reservoir at the mouth of Snowstorm Canyon.

Incident Objectives:

  • Provide safety for first responders and the public through risk analysis and hazard mitigation.
  • Minimize acres burned utilizing direct extinguishment tactics.
  • Utilize resources where they can be most successful and ensure tactics have a high probability of success.
  • Protect and minimize impacts to communities, private property, infrastructure, cultural, natural resources and Sage Grouse habitat.
  • Strengthen collaboration and relationships with cooperators, ranchers, tribal communities, and the public by delivering accurate information while seeking opportunities to build new relationships.

Evacuation Orders:

  • Evacuation Orders: All Evacuation Orders have been lifted.  
  • Evacuation Warnings: Zone LAS-553 remains in an evacuation warning.  
  • All other zones have been placed back into a normal status.  
  • Conditions may change rapidly due to changing conditions on this fire, or a new fire.  Be prepared to leave at a moment's notice.
  • Interactive Evacuation Map is available through https://protect.genasys.com/ 

For shelter information call (530) 254-4500: or visit the Lassen County Sheriff's Office Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/LassenSheriff/

  • Interactive Evacuation Map is available through https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/46cb79ef933d4485b9966a9730e2d944/page/Perimeter/ 

Please note that California and Nevada use different, though similar, programs.  Evacuation status information for each state is displayed within their respective programs.  

Area Closures: The Bureau of Land Management has instituted a temporary closure of public lands for the Biscar Fire.  Public lands near Snowstorm Road and Vincent Canyon, northeast of Susanville in Lassen County, are closed for wildland fire fighting operations.  Pursuant to 43 CFR 8364.1, this temporary closure is being implemented for public and firefighter safety during emergency fire suppression actions.  View the Full Closure Order and Map.

Fire Restrictions: The Bureau of Land Management issued seasonal fire restrictions effective July 15th for BLM-managed public lands within Lassen, Modoc, Plumas, Sierra, Siskiyou and Shasta counties in California and Washoe County, Nevada. These seasonal restrictions are in addition to the year-round, statewide fire prevention order. These fire orders for Applegate and Eagle Lake field offices are in place to help prevent wildfires and will remain in effect until further notice.

The fire restrictions prohibit campfires and barbecues except within established campfire rings and barbecue grills in certain designated recreation sites:   Read more at https://www.blm.gov/announcement/blm-announces-seasonal-fire-restrictions-ne-california-nw-nevada-0

About the Bureau of Land Management - Northern California District.  The BLM’s Northern California District manages about 3.5 million acres of public lands, covering a diverse landscape, ranging from the arid and rugged Great Basin to the fog shrouded forests of the North Coast. The Redding-based district office oversees field offices in Alturas, Arcata, Redding and Susanville and a field station in Cedarville. The district contains two distinct regions. On the east, the Applegate and Eagle Lake field offices oversee vast expanses of public lands in a high desert landscape, including about a million and a half acres in far western Nevada. Small communities depend on public lands for economic benefits, primarily through livestock grazing, and tourism uses ranging from hunting to mountain biking. These lands provide habitat for 14 wild horse herds and special status species, such as greater sage grouse. On the west, the Arcata and Redding field offices manage smaller, scattered blocks of public land with more emphasis on recreation demands from urban areas.

title: Ptarmigan Fire
field_incident_description:
Ptarmigan Fire Daily Update
August 25, 2026
Quick Facts
Size: 24,770
Cause: Lightning
Location: 20 miles NW of Mazama, WA
Containment: 55
Personnel: 42

Overview: Fire behavior remained moderate, with some backing fire activity on the southern edge of the fire’s perimeter and interior consumption of un-burned fuels. Scattered heat was confined to the Middle and West Forks of the Pasayten River. Road repair continues on Harts Pass Road (FSR) 5400. Fire activity on the Ptarmigan Fire has been minimal and is expected to remain minimal. No further updates will be issued unless there is an increase in fire behavior.

Operations: Mastication work continues along Forest Service Road (FSR) 52. Crews will be working on repair work along Harts Pass Road (FSR) 54. Local crews will remain available to support initial attack efforts on new fires near the Ptarmigan Fire including those from the recent lightning.

Safety and Closures: FSR 5400 Harts Pass Road has re-opened, but all trails north of Harts Pass are still closed, including the Pacific Crest Trail from milepost 2626.6 near Harts Pass north to the Canadian border. Although fire activity has slowed, warmer temperatures may result in increased activity and the fire is still burning within 3 miles of the Pacific Crest Trail near Holman Pass. This section of trail is remote with no easy access and limited ability for search and rescue personnel to respond in the event of increased fire activity. The fire team continues to monitor conditions and evaluate closure needs. The public is asked to continue to avoid FSR 5200 while operations are winding down as there is still heavy machinery working on the road. Several closures remain in place on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. Please be advised that road repair work is also underway on Harts Pass Road. Level 2 fire restrictions remain in effect. More details: http://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/okanogan-wenatchee

Fire Weather: Tuesday will be sunny, with high temperatures of 70-80, relative humidity of 19-25%, and mild diurnal terrain driven winds. Continued southerly progression in the Middle and West Forks of the Pasayten River and Rock Creek is possible. Wednesday will be mostly clear and breezy. High temperatures will reach mid-80s in the valleys, mid-70s in the mountains, and west wind up to 10 mph. Continued southerly progression in the Middle and West Forks of the Pasayten River and Rock Creek is possible.

Smoke: A daily smoke outlook is being produced for the area by an incident air resource advisor. That outlook can be found at: https://outlooks.airfire.org/outlook/9b4664c3?. Additional information on current smoke hazard levels can be found at https://fire.airnow.gov/#6/41/-98

Evacuations: There are no current evacuations in place for this fire. For more information, visit the Okanogan County Emergency Management page. https://www.okanogancounty.gov/

Ptarmigan Fire Information
InciWeb: https://inciweb.wildfire.gov/waowf-ptarmigan-fire
Facebook: Ptarmigan Fire Information 2026 - https://www.facebook.com/ptarmiganfireinfo2026/
Fire Information Line: 509-215-8214 | Hours: 8 AM to 8 PM
Fire E-mail: 2026.ptarmigan@firenet.gov
field_incident_overview:
The Ptarmigan Fire was discovered on July 17th, 2026. That morning it was called in by a member of the public and Goat Peak Lookout, and confirmed by a reconnaissance flight over the Pasayten Wilderness. It is located 20 miles NW of Mazama, Washington, near the Canadian border. It is burning in the old Tatoosh fire area. Smokejumpers staffed the fire on July 18th, and have conducted historic structure protection in the area. An Okanogan-Wenatchee Type 3 team was assigned to manage the fire on July 25th, 2026 after significant growth occurred. The fire moved southward to burn around the Pasayten Airstrip and became established in the Middle Fork Pasayten River drainage, progressing toward Point Defiance. The northern section burned across the Canadian border in two places to the east of Monument 83 historic lookout.  Management of the Ptarmigan Fire transitioned to a Type 4 organization at 8:30 a.m. Sunday. Fire behavior has remained moderate. Fire movement is minimal, and heat is confined to the Middle and West Forks of the Pasayten River. Road repair continues on Harts Pass Road (FSR) 5400. 

Evacuations: There are no current evacuations in place for this fire. For more information on evacuations, please visit the Okanogan County Emergency Management page. https://www.okanogancounty.gov/1861/ACTIVE-INCIDENTS

title: Castle
field_incident_overview:
August 14, 2026 will be the final update for the Castle Fire unless there is a change in fire behavior. 

The Castle Fire was first reported on July 22, 2026.  It is currently estimated to be 3,613 acres and 94% contained.  

Fire Activity: Firefighters continue to mop up and patrol for any heat sources. Rehab work, chipping, and back hauling equipment from the fireline will be conducted. The fire is being managed for full suppression. 

For additional information about wildfires, closures, and restrictions, visit the Umpqua National Forest Facebook page https://www.facebook.com/UmpquaNationalForest or call Tiller Ranger District at 541-825-3100.

Fire Weather: Temperatures will gradually warm by 1 or 2 degrees each day, peaking Sunday and Monday at about 5 degrees above normal. Daytime humidity will lower gradually as well, but overnight recoveries will remain good. Winds across the area will continue the diurnal pattern, with light downslope/down-valley flows overnight, and breezy upslope/up-valley in the afternoons. Ridges will see light N-NE winds overnight, with breezy W-NW afternoon winds. Thunderstorm chances will be very low through the weekend, with most mid-level moisture and instability shifted to the east of the area, but with the trough overhead, a highly isolated storm is possible. Temperatures are expected to cool again, humidity should improve, and thunderstorm chances creep up early next week when the trough returns.

All National Forest System lands, roads and trails will be closed to public within the closure area. The closure will remain in effect until conditions allow for reopening.  Visit the Umpqua Alerts and Notices page at  https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/umpqua/alerts/castle-fire-closure - You may also click on the Closure Order (pdf) and Closure Order Map (pdf). 

Public Use Restrictions:  As of Friday, July 24, 2026 the Umpqua National Forest moved to Public Use Restrictions (PURs) Stage 2 across the whole Forest. In PURs Stage 2, campfires in wilderness and public firewood cutting (with an internal combustion engine) will no longer be allowed. Campfires within Forest Service-constructed concrete or metal fire rings within designated developed recreation sites are exempt.  More Information is available at https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/umpqua/alerts/public-use-restrictions-stage-2 

Smoke Impacts: With a significant number of fires burning within Oregon, please take steps to protect yourself from smoke.  Smoke can irritate the eyes and lungs and worsen some medical conditions. People most at risk include infants and young children, people with heart or lung disease, older adults and pregnant people.  Smoke levels can change rapidly depending on weather. Check current conditions on the U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality Response Program, the Oregon Smoke Information Blog, DEQ’s Air Quality Index, or by downloading the free OregonAIR app on your smartphone.

About the Forest: The Umpqua National Forest protects 982,510 acres of forest across Douglas, Lane, and Jackson Counties. High Cascades glaciation, whitewater rapids, and explosive volcanic events have shaped the Forest's spectacular scenery and abundant natural resources. Verdant stands of hemlock, fir and cedar transition to forests of mixed conifers and hardwoods at lower elevations, while alpine ecosystems dominate high peaks like Mount Thielsen. The Forest's waterways and diverse ecosystems create desirable habitat for many species of fish and wildlife, in addition to providing outstanding recreational opportunities to our local communities and visitors.

The Forest is headquartered in Roseburg and has four ranger districts: Cottage Grove, Diamond Lake, North Umpqua, and Tiller. The Forest is also the home of the Dorena Genetic Research Center and Wolf Creek Job Corps Center. The Dorena Center, located in Cottage Grove, houses breeding programs for disease-resistant trees, a native plant development program, and the National Tree Climbing Program. The Wolf Creek Job Corps in Glide is a federal tuition-free training and education program.

title: Big Grass Fire
field_incident_description: The Big Grass Fire started on July 23, 2026, following a lightning strike. Fuels within the fire area consist primarily of brush, short grasses, and tall grasses, providing a continuous fuel bed capable of supporting fire spread under favorable weather conditions. The landscape is characterized by steep, rugged canyons interspersed with dry creek drainages and remote, inaccessible terrain. These conditions create significant challenges for firefighter access and ground-based suppression operations. The combination of steep topography, receptive grass and brush fuels, and limited accessibility can contribute to increased fire behavior and complicate containment efforts, particularly during periods of elevated temperatures, low relative humidity, and increased winds.
field_incident_overview:
The Big Grass Fire was reported on July 23, 2026, following a lightning strike. Fuels in the area consist of brush, short grasses, and tall grasses. The fire exhibited extreme fire behavior, with rapid rates of spread in all directions when smoke lifted and winds picked up in the afternoon.

Numerous residential structures, outbuildings, and associated improvements were threatened. Additional values at risk include the Wild and Scenic River corridor, North Fork Campground, Three Forks Campground, priority sage-grouse habitat, essential pronghorn habitat, grazing allotments, a Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS), the South Mountain communication site, and numerous mining operations farther north. Continued fire spread has the potential to impact residential properties, critical infrastructure, recreational facilities, wildlife habitat, rangeland resources, and fire weather monitoring capabilities.

California Interagency Incident Management Team 5 assumed command of the Big Grass Fire July 28, 2026. Northwest Complex Incident Management Team 10 (NW10) assumed command of the fire August 11, 2026.

title: Porcupine Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Porcupine Fire was discovered on the evening of July 24th and is believed to be a holdover fire from a previous lightning storm. It is burning in steep terrain with cliffs, rock screes, and subalpine fir, located approximately two miles east of Porcupine Lake. People who live and recreate in the area should remain aware of this incident and the potential for changing conditions. Firefighting personnel will be using Porcupine Lake Trail #642 to access the fire area. Lake Pend Oreille and Porcupine Lake will act as a dip site for air resources. Exercise caution and yield to firefighting aircraft.

The first shift saw initial attack firefighters inserted into the area by helicopter. It took crews almost two days to saw in an access route through heavy brush, and dead and down timber. With support from scoopers and helicopters, firefighters were able to directly engage the fire. Firefighters constructed handline around most of the fire, but they were unable to "anchor" at the base of the fire because of its location on a cliff. Due to terrain, issues with escape routes, and no feasible safety zones or medevac sites, further direct effort proved unsuccessful and unsafe. The handline held the fire at 3.5 acres until a wind event and rollouts on the cliff face resulted in further fire spread. The current suppression strategy is to confine the fire to an area that limits the threat to values at risk, including a communication site, recreation infrastructure, and of course nearby communities and private property.

title: Sand Creek
field_incident_overview:
The Sand Creek Fire was first discovered 7.5 miles southeast of Wisdom in the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest in rugged remote terrain.  The fire was estimated at 40 acres upon first size up. Firefighters first observed crowning and torching in live green and dead and down subalpine fir. Smokejumpers were inserted and local resources responded with hotshot crews and heavy equipment. 

The Sand Creek Fire continued to grow in a southern direction aided by multiple consecutive days of Critical Fire Weather beginning August 5.  The fire continued south as terrain driven conditions pushed it into eastern oriented drainages. Beginning August 6, the fire doubled in size daily and began a rapid advancement east towards the Pioneer Mountains Scenic Byway and Grasshopper Valley.  The Beaverhead County Sheriff ordered evacuations for select residents on August 8.  The Pioneer Mountains Scenic Byway remains closed.

Priorities for the incident include firefighter and public safety, protection of private lands, and safeguarding critical infrastructure in the surrounding area.

title: Double Springs Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Double Springs Fire is a lightning-caused wildfire burning approximately 21 miles southeast of Challis, Idaho, in the Christian Gulch area of the Salmon-Challis National Forest. The fire was detected on July 24, 2026, and is burning in steep, rugged terrain with heavy timber, dead and down fuels, and limited road access.

Since the fire was discovered, firefighters have implemented a full suppression strategy focused on protecting firefighter and public safety while minimizing fire growth. Due to the steep slopes, loose shale, and challenging terrain, suppression efforts have relied on a combination of existing road systems, natural barriers, and strategically constructed containment lines rather than direct attack in some portions of the fire.

Throughout the incident, weather conditions have played a significant role in fire behavior. Periods of hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and gusty winds have resulted in increased fire activity, while cooler temperatures, higher humidity, and overnight inversions have moderated fire behavior and allowed crews to strengthen containment lines and improve access into the fire area.

This 15 member incident management team is here to lend their expertise with the Northern Rockies Team 2 in managing the Three Queens, King, Goat, Grand Park 2, and Wonderland Complex Fires for the next 14 days before heading back to Australia and New Zealand. The Three Queens fire is burning primarily in high elevation subalpine fir stringers above Lake Kachess. Wind driven fire behavior persists as strong winds push flames across fuels. Fire activity has increased in areas where fuels, wind, and topography have aligned, producing periods of faster fire spread. This mountainous region also exhibits extreme slopes, unstable terrain and rolling material. Crews are monitoring these conditions closely and adjusting tactics to maintain safe and effective operations.

title: Timber Fire
field_incident_overview:
Daily Update (pdf)  ENGLISH     SPANISH     |     Daily Public Information Map (Pdf)     |     Video Links     |     Facebook    |     Smoke Outlook for Timber / Plaskett Fires

A successful community meeting was held yesterday at the Cachagua Community Park.  California Complex Incident Management Team 3 and local community leaders met with around 200 community members for a discussion about the Timber Fire.

A live stream of the event is available at  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8L-hSCwTDdg 

The Timber Fire was detected around 9:30 in the evening on Saturday, August 8. It is primarily burning east of the Big Sur Coastline and into the rugged Ventana Wilderness.  The fire is burning within the 2016 Soberanes Fire, with a mix of older fire killed fuels, and much younger regrowth.  It was last mapped at 24,727 acres and 21% contained (Slight decrease in acres due to better mapping)

CURRENT SITUATION:
The Timber Fire showed some activity on its southeast corner near Partington Ridge as winds picked up overnight. However, night crews along the highway were able to quickly extinguish and mop up hot spots, and overall the highway edge and the road into Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park looked good and cold. 

Assignments today will continue as they have for the last few days, with heavy equipment opening roads and containment lines from previous fires and hotshot crews accessing and opening areas that the dozers are unable to reach. Hotshots are being supported in remote areas by helicopter, including by line medics, who have been flown out to ensure that any injuries on the line receive quick care. 

Aviation Operations: Two dedicated Air Attack platforms are assigned to the incident, supported by Type 1 (Heavy Lift) and Type 2 (Medium lift) helicopters and both day and night Uncrewed Aircraft System (UAS) operations.  Fixed-wing air tanker availability may be limited due to high national demand. Available aviation resources will continue supporting ground operations where they can be most effective.

Infrared (IR) flights were unable to fly last night and today due to smoke and cloud cover.  As a result, the current mapped fire perimeter may be inaccurate until updated IR data becomes available.

WEATHER:No major day over day changes forecast with mostly sunny skies. Smoke shading will be more prevalent on the Plaskett fire. Temperatures running near or a few degrees below normal, mainly in the mid 70s to mid 80s. Humidity readings will trend more seasonable with afternoon minimums 18-28%. General winds from the Northwest 5-10 mph with afternoon ridgetop gusts to 15 mph. Most of the winds over the fire will be diurnally driven and light under 8 mph. The marine layer depth should be around 2000 feet and confined to the immediate coastline after mixing out by 1000 hours.

CLOSURES AND EVACUATIONS: A 40‑mile stretch of Highway 1 in Big Sur is now closed to support Timber and Plaskett Fire operations.  The closure runs from Gorda (Mile Post 10) -  11.7 mi north of Ragged Point to 9.5 mi north of Big Sur (Mile Post 56). Please avoid unnecessary travel in the area and use US 101 as an alternate route. Electronic signs are in place.

EACUATIONS AND CLOSURES:  Evacuation warnings and orders are in effect. For current information and to sign up for alerts, view the Interactive Evacuation Page and Monterey County's Department of Emergency Management website.  

To directly sign up for Alerts, Visit: https://alertmontereycounty.genasys.com/portal/en

AREA CLOSURE:  The Los Padres National Forest has issued an Area Closure for Forest Service managed lands surrounding the Timber and Plaskett Fires.  Full text of the Closure Order, and Closure Order Map. 

Los Padres National Forest encompasses nearly two million acres of central California's scenic Coast and Transverse Ranges. The forest stretches across almost 220 miles from north to south and consists of two separate land divisions. The northern division is within Monterey County and northern San Luis Obispo County and includes the beautiful Big Sur Coast and scenic interior areas. The "main division" of the forest includes lands within San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Ventura and Kern Counties.

title: Weiser Knoll Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Weiser Knoll Fire is located 13 miles southeast of Lander, Wyoming.  

The cause of the fire remains under investigation and no further information about the cause will be available until the investigation concludes. 

The Weiser Knoll Fire was reported on the afternoon of Aug. 9, 2026, at approximately 2:15 p.m,  the fire spread rapidly through grass and sagebrush fuels under severe red flag conditions and strong wind gusts. Initial response was led by U.S. Wildland Fire Service, local cooperators and other federal agencies who worked together to aggressively to protect life, property, and natural and cultural resources. As the fire escalated, additional federal wildland crews, heavy equipment, and aviation resources were assigned to continue suppression operations. Supported by recent favorable weather, firefighters have been successful halting the fire's forward progress and establishing solid control lines bringing the containment to 95%. The perimeter of the fire was updated using detailed satellite imagery, and fire size has been changed to 15,817 acres.

title: Sisi Fire
field_incident_overview:
The Sisi Fire is located in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, within a remote, steep, and rugged mountainous landscape. The surrounding area consists of forested slopes, drainages, and variable terrain near the communities of Lucerne, Holden Village, and Stehekin. The fire is burning in a mosaic of timber, timber understory, brush, and partially cured grasses, with abundant snags and heavy dead and down fuels. Fire behavior remains active, including backing, flanking, uphill and up-drainage runs, group tree torching, and spotting. The greatest potential for growth remains along the southern and eastern portions of the fire where active heat, continuous fuels, and steep terrain align.

 The U.S. Forest Service initiated an aggressive initial attack on the Sisi Fire using a Type 1 helicopter and rappeller support following a mid-August lightning storm. Although aerial firefighters achieved early success, progress halted due to severe hazards, including tree torching and rolling debris on 50% slopes. These conditions forced crews to disengage for their own safety. Following four days of active suppression efforts, critical fire weather triggered significant growth on August 20. Little Giant Fire resources will continue to respond and strategize its containment.

A full-suppression strategy is being utilized, with tactics focused on keeping the fire within the smallest practicable footprint while providing the highest probability of success and minimizing risk to firefighters and aviators. Values at risk include Lucerne, Holden Village, Stehekin, recreation resources, infrastructure, and other natural and cultural resources. The Pacific Crest Trail remains closed between the North Cascades National Park/Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary and High Bridge along the Agnes Creek portion of the trail.

Updates on alerts and evacuations can be obtained here on the Chelan County Emergency Management Facebook page, or the website at https://www.co.chelan.wa.us/emergency-management/pages/active-emergencies.

title: 2026 Electric Fire - MBS
field_incident_overview:
A series of thunderstorms over several weeks brought a significant amount of lightning activity to the Mount Baker-Snouqualmie National Forest. During one of these events, the Electric Fire was reported on Aug. 22 at 7:30 p.m. The fire is located seven miles north of Marblemount, Washington, burning within the Bacon Creek drainage on the Mount Baker Ranger District. It was originally estimated at 15 acres; the fire was burning in heavy fuels, including dead and down timber, in steep, rugged terrain that significantly limited safe access for firefighters. The Prineville Hotshots supported by aviation resources were dispatched for the initial attack. From Aug. 22–23, additional storms passed through the area. Following these storms, easterly winds on Aug. 24–5 further dried out the landscape. 

On Aug. 26, westerly winds arrived, and the fire grew into its current footprint. These winds pushed the fire through the heavier fuels and difficult terrain, contributing to the expansion.

title: Plaskett Fire
field_incident_overview:
Daily Update (PDF)     |    Morning Update Spanish     |     Daily Maps (PDF)     |     Video Updates     |     Smoke Updates

 

The Plaskett fire was discovered on August 27, 2026 at around 9:30 AM.  It began burning in a remote and inaccessible area on the southern part of the Monterey District, which allowed the fire to outpace initial attack.  It is currently estimated at 15,478 acres. 

CURRENT SITUATION:
The Plaskett Fire was active all night, and firefighters remained in engaged in structure defense along the Los Burros road overnight, supported by night flying aircraft. Rocks rolling onto Highway 1 remains a concern. 

Fire crews near Sand Dollar and Plaskett creek executed tactical firing operations overnight as the fire backed toward structures and residences. Firefighters maintained the perimeter near Plaskett Creek, while northern teams opened existing road systems and installed hose lines. On the eastern front, the fire reached the length of the primary dozer line, crossing South Coast Road and resulting in several slop-overs into Fort Hunter Liggett. Ground teams, supported by multiple fuel cycles from night flying helicopters, engaged these slop-overs and conducted defensive firing near Los Burros Road to protect threatened homes and structures. Additionally, crews identified a new 100-foot by 100-foot spot fire across Buckeye Road in the Willow Creek drainage.

Priorities for fire operations during the day are the protection of residential areas along the Los Burros ridge and toward Alder Creek. Crews will work to contain the small spot fire while scouting terrain further east of the ridge roads to establish new secondary fuel breaks. Operations will also continue to monitor fire spread backing toward Highway 1 to improve protection for coastal structures.

Today, a large resource surge will continue, with firefighters reporting to logistical bases established to support both fires at Haystack, Big Sur, and at Plaskett.  A Mobile Retardant Base is being established on the east side of the fire to assist with aerial support on the fire’s east side. The fire has backed down to Highway 1 and firefighters have continued to focus on structure protection as the fire remains active. A large surge of resources continues to arrive on-scene at the fire. 
The fire gained the most acreage on the eastern side burning toward Fort Hunter Liggett and to the south, where firefighters are actively engaged in structure defense on Los Burros Road. Night flying helicopters are in place for continued structure protection overnight.
Crews not engaged with structure protection continue to open CONTAINMENT line along Prewitt Ridge and along the South Coast Ridge Road. With no fire history in the area in more than 50 years, heavy vegetation is driving the active fire behavior. 
Weather over the next few days is expected to trend cooler with higher humidity. Firefighters will take advantage of favorable conditions to look for every opportunity possible to use direct containment tactics.

WEATHER: No major day over day changes forecast with mostly sunny skies. Smoke shading will be more prevalent on the Plaskett fire. Temperatures running near or a few degrees below normal, mainly in the mid 70s to mid 80s. Humidity readings will trend more seasonable with afternoon minimums 18-28%. General winds from the Northwest 5-10 mph with afternoon ridgetop gusts to 15 mph. Most of the winds over the fire will be diurnally driven and light under 8 mph. The marine layer depth should be around 2000 feet and confined to the immediate coastline after mixing out by 1000 hours.

Road CLOSURES AND EVACUATIONS: A hard road closure is in effect on State Route 1:  For updates, visit:  https://roads.dot.ca.gov/?roadnumber=1 or https://quickmap.dot.ca.gov/

Monterey County has issued evacuation warnings and orders.  View the Interactive Evacuation Page For current information and to sign up for alerts visit Monterey County's Department of Emergency Management website.  

San Luis Obispo County has issued Evacuation Warnings for areas effected by the Plaskett Fire - Visit https://www.readyslo.org/emergency/current-protective-actions/ for additional information.

AREA CLOSURE:  The Los Padres National Forest has issued an Area Closure for Forest Service managed lands surrounding the Timber and Plaskett Fires.  Full text of the Closure Order, and Closure Order Map. 

Los Padres National Forest encompasses nearly two million acres of central California's scenic Coast and Transverse Ranges. The forest stretches across almost 220 miles from north to south and consists of two separate land divisions. The northern division is within Monterey County and northern San Luis Obispo County and includes the beautiful Big Sur Coast and scenic interior areas. The "main division" of the forest includes lands within San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara, Ventura and Kern Counties.
